definitions.note: an adjectival phrase describing a face, here one with no beard covering it

parts.note: to clear something is to clean it, so clears gives cleans
a harbour is a haven, a safe place for ships

explanation.surface: Someone tidies up a port, removing every landmark that could be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a harbour being emptied of landmarks. In fact the definition describes a face: one with no beard, so its features are all on show.
explanation.definitionFit: A face with no beard or moustache leaves its features on show, so the definition loosely describes a man who has shaved off all facial hair.

clue.text: Half lost, arrive noisily with medical assistance

definitions.note: the definition names the help, while the answer is the person who provides it

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word is its first two letters, and here half the word lost is kept
noisily says the word that follows is to be heard rather than spelt, so its sound is written another way

parts.note: to arrive is to come

explanation.surface: Someone who has half lost their way turns up loudly, bringing a doctor along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' keeps LO from 'lost'. 'Noisily' turns COME (arrive) into CUM, which sounds the same. A locum is a doctor who stands in for another, so the definition names the help rather than the person.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-in doctor covering for an absent colleague provides temporary medical help in a practice.

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for time within the words a jumbo

parts.note: jumbo means very big, or large

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a spare hour aboard a jumbo jet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo' suggests an aircraft or an elephant, but here it just means LARGE. 'In' puts T (time) inside A LARGE, straight after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An escaped animal or criminal still at large has not been caught, so it is free.

clue.text: Devious youth leader supporting group of workers

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece that supports another sits beneath it, so it comes after

parts.note: a shift is a group of workers on duty together

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here the first letter of youth

explanation.surface: A dishonest young ringleader is backing a team of factory workers.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' puts the Y (the first letter of 'youth', picked by 'leader') under SHIFT, so it comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with an evasive, untrustworthy look seems sly and dishonest.

clue.text: Father's back before mother, say — that's obvious!

indicators.note: back says the word for father is read from its end to its start

parts.note: Pa is an informal word for father
a mother is an example of a parent, which the say signals

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that Dad came home before Mum, as if this were plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns the short word for father round, and 'say' marks mother as just one example of the wider family word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something apparent is plain to see, so calling a thing obvious is a close synonym.

clue.text: Most of team took in raise

indicators.note: most of a word means all of it but its final letter, so the synonym for team loses its tail

parts.note: a cricket or football team is an eleven
to take in food is to eat it, so took in gives ate

explanation.surface: Most of the squad swallowed a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' drops the last letter of ELEVEN (a team in cricket or football) to leave ELEVE, and ATE (took in) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To elevate is to lift something up, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: The polish of one unable to see game?

indicators.note: the X of Y puts Y's name first as a possessive, so the polishing word comes last

parts.note: one unable to see is a blind man, made possessive by the of that precedes it
to buff is to polish, and a buff is a polishing

explanation.surface: Someone asks how a sightless person keeps a shine on things, ending with a playful query.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' reverses the clue's order: the polish of a blind man is a blind man's buff. Blind man's buff is a children's game in which a blindfolded player tries to catch the others.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's party pastime in which a blindfolded player gropes to catch the others is a game.

parts.note: rum is an old British word meaning odd or strange

explanation.surface: A drink of English rum could start a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink but is the adjective, a British colloquialism for odd. Estrange is a verb, so the definition is 'arouse hostility', with 'might' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange people is to alienate them, turning friends into enemies and causing ill feeling.

parts.note: a hazard here is a guess, as in hazarding one, and the university part is the schooling that informs it

explanation.surface: Someone wonders about a danger of student life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazard' suggests a danger, but as a verb it means to venture a guess. The university supplies the education behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A guess grounded in knowledge, the sort a schooled mind makes, is a reasoned estimate rather than a wild stab.

definitions.meaning: an anaesthetic numbing only one area of the body
a pub, especially the one nearest a person's home

explanation.surface: Someone finds a numbing drug in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'public house' is a British pub, and your nearest one is your local.
explanation.definitionFit: A numbing injection for one part of the body is a local anaesthetic, and a person's nearby regular pub is called their local.

clue.text: One married and did the ironing, deeply affected

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: A newlywed did the household ironing and was moved by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' gives I, the Roman numeral, and 'married' gives M, as in genealogies.
explanation.definitionFit: Being strongly moved or struck by something is the sense of the adjective; a stirring speech leaves its audience moved.

clue.text: Someone who numbers true Roman ruins

indicators.note: ruins says the letters of true Roman are wrecked and rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: A counter of things vouches for genuine Roman remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruins' looks like a noun for Roman remains but works as the anagram signal on TRUE ROMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: One who counts or enumerates things is a counter, which is the word's literal sense though it now usually means the top of a fraction.

indicators.note: filled with says the words Bureau richly hold the answer inside them

explanation.surface: A writing desk lavishly stuffed with gold coins.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the two words, from the end of 'Bureau' into 'richly'. 'Gold' is read as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Auric is an adjective for anything made of or relating to the precious yellow metal, from its Latin name aurum.

clue.text: Cartoonist and his boss in a tangle

parts.note: Matt is the Daily Telegraph's long-running pocket cartoonist
a newspaper cartoonist's boss is the editor, abbreviated ED

explanation.surface: A newspaper cartoonist and his editor get into a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: MATT (Matt Pritchett) drew the Telegraph's front-page pocket cartoon, so the clue nods to its own paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair or fibres that are matted are knotted into a dense mess, which is what being tangled means.

clue.text: Bird that's cooked to suit me

indicators.note: cooked suggests the words to suit me are cooked up, worked into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A small bird has been roasted just as the diner likes it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like it describes the bird but is the anagram signal on TO SUIT ME.
explanation.definitionFit: The tit, a small songbird, is also called by this older full name.

clue.text: Web doctor needs energy and time

parts.note: an intern is a junior hospital doctor, chiefly in American usage
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A doctor in a web of commitments needs more energy and hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' tempts as an anagram signal, but here it just means INTERN, a junior hospital doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: The worldwide web runs over the global computer network, and the two are loosely interchangeable names.

definitions.meaning: describes a clause or term broad enough to take in every possible case
read literally, a policing goal of seizing every offender

explanation.surface: Someone describes an insurance policy against crime.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition, with its question mark, splits the answer into a phrase: catch all the criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch-all provision covers every eventuality, and a police force that nabbed every criminal would be catching them all.

indicators.note: failing suggests the words on a Latin go wrong and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pupil is failing an exam on a Latin topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' tempts as a school subject, given 'Latin', but it means a citizen of a state.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of a particular country, such as a British subject, is a national of that state.

parts.note: someone who is out is absent, not at home
a family line is a person's descendants

explanation.surface: Someone tries to track down relatives who are missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trace' looks like a verb about finding people, but it means to draw round a shape.
explanation.definitionFit: To trace a shape is to draw its contour, so the two verbs share that sense.

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race
the end of something is its conclusion

explanation.surface: Someone reaches the final stage of a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests the theatre, but it is a stretch of a journey, a LEG.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional tale handed down, often of heroes and uncertain truth, is a kind of story.

parts.note: the States is the common name for the United States of America

explanation.surface: Someone describes property on the US East Coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lands' looks like a verb (an aircraft touching down) but is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Large country properties owned by one family are landed holdings, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Animal that might fly — given time!

definitions.text: Animal that might fly — given time!

parts.note: the saying pigs might fly mocks something that will never happen
an eon is a vast stretch of time

explanation.surface: Someone jokes that a pig could take wing if it only had long enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a PIG (from the saying 'pigs might fly') given an EON of time to evolve might become this flying bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A common grey bird famed for flying home over great distances really is a creature that takes to the air.

clue.text: Swell in second class aboard ship

indicators.note: aboard puts a passenger inside the vessel, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a boat is a ship, loosely

indicators.note: second picks out the second letter of the word class

explanation.surface: A passenger in a lower class of cabin rides out the waves at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second class' reads as a ticket grade, but 'second' picks out L, the second letter of 'class'. 'Aboard' puts that L inside BOAT, and 'Swell', which suggests the sea, is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bloat is to puff up or distend, so both verbs mean to grow larger.

indicators.note: sort of hints at a loose version of the words A neurotic, their letters shuffled into a new word

explanation.surface: An anxious kind of soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests a person's character, matching 'neurotic', but it is a strong drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An orange-flavoured French liqueur is an alcoholic spirit.

parts.note: eras are periods of time

indicators.note: start picks out the opening letter of the word express

explanation.surface: Someone cancels departures and puts on an express train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Express' suggests a fast train, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase writing is to rub it out, which wipes out or cancels it.

indicators.note: broke suggests the words sat in café are smashed and reassembled in another order

explanation.surface: A penniless person sits at the door of a café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' reads as a doorway, but it is the verb, stressed on its second syllable: to enchant.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to hold them spellbound, which is exactly what it means to captivate them.

indicators.note: flipping turns the word for clever over so it is read from its end

parts.note: smart means clever

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at some ingenious ways of getting about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British oath ('flipping clever!') but is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Streetcars running on rails carry passengers, so they are a means of public transport.

clue.text: Helped rinse dish to be filled again

indicators.note: to dish something is to ruin it, so the letters of Helped rinse are wrecked and remade

explanation.surface: Someone helped rinse a bowl so it could be topped up once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' looks like the crockery being rinsed but is a verb meaning to ruin, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Restocked or topped up to the brim once more, as a glass is refilled.
